abstract: Neuronal hyperexcitability (NHE) can leave lasting consequences in neuronal circuits. It is often assumed that hyperexcitable neurons give rise to hyperactive networks. Here we asked how a single injection of kainic acid, which induces NHE without seizures, reshapes the hippocampal-cortical circuit at the cellular and network levels two months later. Using high-density microelectrode arrays in acute slices, we found a long-lasting reduction in spontaneous firing and bursting across the hippocampal regions, a lower proportion of active electrodes throughout the circuit, and weaker coupling from CA1 to the entorhinal cortex. In contrast, whole-cell recordings revealed region- and cell-type-specific changes in intrinsic excitability. CA1 and CA3 pyramidal neurons and CA3 interneurons exhibited increased evoked firing, whereas CA1 interneurons exhibited reduced evoked firing. Deep-layer entorhinal neurons, however, received less excitatory synaptic input and fired less. Thus, network and cellular alterations were dissociated after NHE. Finally, a pharmacological challenge with the GluK1 agonist ATPA revealed region-specific changes in network responsiveness, with a blunted response in CA3 and enhanced response in the non-entorhinal cortex, with no differences in DG, CA1 or entorhinal cortex. These findings suggest that, after the induction of NHE, region- and cell-type-specific neuronal remodeling coexists with reduced network activity ex vivo, and that the state of the circuit cannot be inferred from the properties of its individual neurons.
